# Skills fix plan and outcome, 2026-11-28

Follows `2026-11-28-skills-review.md`. Three stages: an Opus agent per overlapping skill pair settled the boundary, an Opus agent
per skill planned every finding (apply, skip or defer), and a Sonnet agent per skill applied the plan and re-ran the evals on
`anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5`. Finding ids are the order of the findings in the review document.

## Outcome

- Findings: 722 applied, 141 skipped, 43 deferred. 158 descriptions rewritten, all at most 700 characters.
- Overlaps: 71 of 171 reported pairs were judged real and got a boundary decision.
- Scores below are the implementing agents' own 3-run numbers.

## Retired and deleted (decided after the run)

- Retired with their evals: `gh-readme` (covered by `readme`), `git-flow` and `trunk-based` (covered by `branching-models`).
- `branching-models` got its trunk-based section back from before the run, since its plan had moved that content to the now retired `trunk-based` skill. The description names trunk-based work again; that wording is untested.
- Deleted reference files that no SKILL.md points at any more: `aws/references/cli.md`, `game-craft/references/` (8 files), `feature-flags/references/flag-hygiene.md`, `forgejo-cli/references/issues.md`, `branching-models/references/hubflow.md`, `pr-comments/references/forgejo.md`, `docs-audit/references/one-fact.md`, `api-oauth-provider/references/api-key-storage.md`, `goff/references/sdk-overview.md`, `nuget/references/` (3 files).
- Deleted as duplicates of a sibling skill's copy: `dotnet-diagnostics` (3 files, in `dotnet-performance`), `goff` (13 files, in `goff-flags`, `goff-relay-proxy`, `goff-sdk`), `fresh-eyes/references/tunnel.md`, `handoff/references/catchup.md`, `modernize/references/sunset.md`.
- The per-skill sections for `gh-readme`, `git-flow` and `trunk-based` below are kept as a record of what was planned.

## Boundary decisions

- android-build owns R8 build and runtime failures: release-only ClassNotFoundException or NoSuchMethodError, missing or wrong keep rules for one failure, and minify or shrink settings in the build types. android-performance owns Macrobenchmark, Baseline Profiles and app-size measurement (APK Analyzer, resources, native libraries, ABIs). It records whether R8 ran and the size before and after, but sends any R8 failure to android-build. Both skills already send keep-rule audits and DEX size reduction to the external `android-skills:r8-analyzer`, and that stays as it is.
- api-keys owns API keys a platform issues to its consumers: format, hash-only storage, scopes, rotation, revocation and ownership. api-webhooks owns webhook signing secrets from start to finish: the signing scheme, per-endpoint secret generation, storage, and rotation by overlapping signatures. It already has the rotation procedure in references/signing.md, and api-keys' hash-only storage cannot work for a secret the sender has to read back to sign with. Neither eval suite contains the other skill's prompts, so no eval changes are needed.
- kotlin owns one-shot event delivery: choosing between SharedFlow, Channel and consumed state, and an event that is dropped, replayed or split, including a navigation event lost while the screen starts. Its Flow section and references/flow.md hold the procedure for this. android keeps lifecycle-aware collection (repeatOnLifecycle, collectAsStateWithLifecycle, a collector that keeps running while the screen is stopped) and restoration through SavedStateHandle after process death. It points to kotlin for event semantics. Tie-break: if the question is why the event vanished or what type to use, that is kotlin. If the question is when the UI subscribes or what survives a killed process, that is android.
- api-keys owns everything about keys the platform issues: the keys-versus-OAuth decision for its own consumers, plus key format, hash-only storage and lookup, scopes, rotation, revocation and ownership. api-oauth-provider owns the authorization-server (issuer) side once OAuth is chosen, meaning third-party apps or agents acting for users: grants, PKCE, tokens, refresh rotation, OAuth scopes, consent, client registration, discovery and MCP auth. It points to api-keys for the keys decision and for key storage. The api-keys suite keeps the route-keys-vs-auth prompt as its positive trigger.
- aspire owns everything about an Aspire app: the AppHost (Program.cs/apphost.cs resource wiring such as AddProject/AddPostgres/WithReference/WaitFor), ServiceDefaults, integrations, the aspire CLI, startup or connection failures under aspire run, and publish/deploy. csharp owns general C# language and .NET code quality inside the services (types, nullability, async, DI/options/logging in the generic host) and points to aspire for AppHost and orchestration work, because csharp's "*.cs" trigger would otherwise catch AppHost files.
- Keep the split both skills already state. ef-core owns EF Core data access: LINQ query shape, N+1, Include/split queries, tracking, bulk updates, DbContext lifetime, migrations and raw SQL/Dapper, even when the query sits in a service an endpoint calls. aspnet-core owns the HTTP layer: endpoints, DTOs, validation, ProblemDetails, OpenAPI, middleware and auth wiring, and it sends data-access work to ef-core. The shared N+1 prompt stays a positive trigger in the ef-core suite.
- aws-cli owns how the CLI command or script itself works: pagination and truncated output, --output/--query, the pager, retries and timeouts, waiters, skeletons and input files, dry runs, client tokens, the write-confirmation procedure, and env keys vs --profile precedence. aws owns who and where you are and what you may do: account, region and identity context, sign-in (SSO, aws login), expired tokens, IAM and AccessDenied, and cost queries. aws points to aws-cli for command mechanics. aws-cli already points to aws for profiles, SSO and IAM.
- aws-resource-query owns read-only questions about what exists in an account, how it is configured and what state it is in now, including the deny list and secret-safe projections. aws-cli owns how a command or script works (pagination, output, retries, timeouts, waiters, skeletons) and the procedure for any state-changing command, including one the user asks for in the middle of a query session. aws keeps credentials, profiles, SSO and IAM.
- api-rest-design owns the HTTP contract side of a change: whether a field rename, removal or type change is breaking, the version scheme, notice windows by audience, the Deprecation/Sunset headers and the written versioning policy. deprecation-migration owns the project of moving consumers off a whole old API version, service, library or feature (keep-or-sunset decision, announce, migrate each consumer, remove once usage is zero), so "sunset the v1 API" with its consumers belongs to it.
- better-auth owns every request about Better Auth's own settings for Redis: the `secondaryStorage` option, what it stores (sessions, verification records, rate-limit counters), `session.storeSessionInDatabase`, and why the session table is empty. redis owns the Redis server side: eviction policy, `maxmemory`, TTLs, key design and persistence for the instance holding those sessions. This is the split both skills already describe; only redis's wording and routing need fixing.
- aws-resource-query owns read-only questions about live resources: what exists, how it is configured, what state it is in, plus the deny list and --query projections for those reads. aws owns account, region and identity context, sign-in, SSO, IAM and AccessDenied debugging, and cost queries. Neither skill owns CLI mechanics, scripts or write commands. Those belong to aws-cli, which has the dry-run, client-token, pagination and waiter procedure. The descriptions already split resource listing from sign-in and IAM this way, and the two suites share no prompt (aws-not-resource-listing is already a negative in aws), so no eval changes are needed.
- branching-models owns every git-flow request: detecting the model, choosing one ("which branching model should we use"), and feature/release/hotfix/support/init procedures with git-flow-next, AVH or plain git. Its body already holds git-flow's whole procedure word for word (same tables, hotfix-with-open-release rule, git-flow-next differences, gotchas, identical reference files) and it was built to replace git-flow, so git-flow is a redundant copy and gets retired, not narrowed.
- branching-models owns the policy part of a backport: which branch a fix lands on, in what order, and whether a release branch should exist at all. In trunk-based that means fix on trunk first, then `cherry-pick -x` onto release/X.Y. In git-flow it means a hotfix plus the merge into an open release branch. git-history owns how a cherry-pick is done: ranges, merge commits (`-m 1`), a conflicted or aborted pick, picking only some files, and every other history rewrite. A bare "backport this fix to release/1.4" goes to git-history, unless the request is about the repo's release-branch workflow or the model's rules.
- vue owns Vue/Pinia/Nuxt bugs that come from a single construct: lost reactivity (destructured store without storeToRefs, a reassigned reactive, a prop copied into a ref), a wrong watcher or computed, or a hydration or fetch problem. click-path-audit owns the case where each function is correct but the ordered sequence a control sets off (handler calls, actions that reset fields they don't own, effects or watchers firing after the click, async races) undoes the result. That applies in any framework, Vue and Pinia included.
- catchup owns every request to brief a returning human from live project state: what changed, what needs them, new terms, next move. It is model-invocable and its SKILL.md holds the procedure. handoff owns carrying work to another agent: writing the handoff document, --bg launch and --recover for a dead session. Its --catchup mode goes away, and `/skill:catchup` is the manual entry point.
- dotnet-native-interop owns every request about the boundary between managed and native code: P/Invoke and LibraryImport declarations, mapping C headers, string and struct marshalling, memory ownership, SafeHandle, callbacks, library loading, DllNotFoundException, EntryPointNotFoundException or AccessViolationException at a native call, and DllImport-to-LibraryImport migration. csharp owns general C# and .NET code with no native boundary. This split already exists in B's "Not for" line (it sends general C# work to `csharp`). Only A is missing the matching pointer back.
- cold-read owns the cold-read procedure: the blind stranger read with a private yardstick, contents passed inline, the three report questions and the verdict scale. It handles every model-routed request of the "would someone new follow this?" kind. fresh-eyes stays a manual-only command (disable-model-invocation), so there is no routing collision, and its --cold flag is only a manual entry point that hands off to cold-read instead of keeping its own copy.
- cold-read owns blind "would a stranger follow this?" reads of any artifact, READMEs included, done by a fresh subagent that only diagnoses. readme owns writing, auditing, scoring, restructuring and beautifying a README. Its optional cold-reader test is a step inside Restructure that hands the read to cold-read, using readme's five questions.
- cold-read owns every blind stand-alone read, including of a README ("would someone new follow this README?", a fresh-eyes read before publishing), because only cold-read's body has the procedure: a fresh subagent, contents passed inline, a yardstick the reviewer never sees, and a verdict. gh-readme owns writing, auditing against its scored checklist, restructuring and beautifying a README. When gh-readme wants the optional cold-reader test, it hands the blind read to cold-read and adds its own five README questions.
- hubflow owns every request about a HubFlow repo: `git hf` commands, a `[hubflow]` config section, "the DataSift flavour of gitflow", and the auto-push, PR-first and -Xtheirs behaviour. Its body has the full procedure (command table, ask-first list, warnings and caveats), and it won 6 of 6 routing runs. branching-models owns detecting a repo's model, plain git-flow (git-flow-next, AVH or plain git), trunk-based work, and the "which model should we use" question. When it detects `[hubflow]`, it hands off to hubflow.
- branching-models owns working out which model a repo uses, choosing a model ("should we use trunk-based or git-flow"), requests that use another model's words (git-flow terms in a trunk repo), and all git-flow and HubFlow procedures. trunk-based owns the work inside a repo already known to be trunk-based: committing to trunk, short-lived branches, feature flags for unfinished work, branch by abstraction, releasing from trunk, and release branches fed by cherry-picks. Its body and references/release.md hold the fuller procedure for these, and it is the only one of the two with evals for them.
- dotnet-performance owns any request about speed or allocations in C#/.NET code: hot-path reviews and anti-pattern scans, BenchmarkDotNet, and SIMD. csharp owns correctness work, including sync-over-async deadlocks reported as hangs or bugs, nullable warnings, async/cancellation design, DI, options and logging. csharp should point performance requests to dotnet-performance, not to dotnet-diagnostics.
- debloat owns compressing correct, current prose: cutting padding, stacked qualifiers, fused sentences, walls of enumeration and nearby restatements while keeping every rule. doc-tidy keeps its --v0 and --reorder modes but stops carrying its own debloat procedure: its --debloat argument just points to /skill:debloat. debloat has the full workflow (pin the artifact, find the bloat, compress, re-read cold, before-finishing checks). Its value cases also show an effect: 1.00 with the skill against 0.33 and 0.13 without. doc-tidy's --debloat mode is a shortened copy whose case barely differs (0.94 with, 0.91 without), and v0-rewrite already sends this work to debloat. The two suites share no prompt, so no positive trigger has to be moved.
- deprecation-migration owns sunsets and deprecations: the sunset-or-keep decision, moving consumers off an API, service, library or feature, removal, zombie code and expand/contract schema changes. modernize owns upgrading, migrating or rewriting a legacy stack (spike, testability milestone, safety ladder, hazards, phased plan). When a modernization plan retires a component in step 6, modernize points to deprecation-migration instead of carrying its own copy.
- devcontainer owns tool versions set through devcontainer.json or Dev Container Features (for example `ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1` with `version`), plus "command not found" in lifecycle commands (userEnvProbe, how the hook is invoked). mise owns requests that touch mise.toml, .tool-versions or mise commands, including when mise runs inside a container.
- deprecation-migration owns the rollout order for a breaking schema change (expand, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, contract, each deployed on its own), on any ORM, Prisma included. prisma owns how Prisma runs it: migration files, checksums, `migrate dev` vs `migrate deploy`, reviewing `--create-only` SQL. For the phased rename/NOT NULL sequence it points to deprecation-migration instead of restating it. No eval prompt is shared, so no suite has to move a case.
- The split already exists in both bodies, so keep it. devils-advocate owns challenges to an idea, strategy, vendor or technology pick, or a conclusion drawn from data, run with the user in the loop through its five modes. doubt-review owns a concrete in-flight artifact or assertion: a diff, a migration, an auth change, or a "this is safe / idempotent / thread-safe" claim. It hands that to a fresh-context subagent before the work is committed. The two eval suites share no prompt, so no case moves.
- reorder owns every move-only reordering job: a list, table, catalog or set of sections put under one principle. Its body has the full procedure (a workflow, rules and a before-finishing check). doc-tidy owns whole-document tidying (--v0, --debloat). Its --reorder mode becomes a short pointer to reorder and no longer restates reorder's rules.
- dotnet-template-authoring owns all `dotnet new` template work: turning a project into a template, template.json symbols, conditions, post-actions and constraints, validation, a template missing from `dotnet new list`, and building a template pack (pack project, content/ layout). nuget owns package versions, CPM, sources, audit, lock files, general `dotnet pack` metadata and publishing any package to nuget.org, template packs included. This is the split dotnet-template-authoring's Not-for line already describes, and its body (steps 1-5, references/packaging.md) has the procedure.
- v0-rewrite owns rewriting a drifted doc as a clean current-state v0, and the v0 rules live only there. It has the full workflow and is the skill the model invokes by itself. doc-tidy stays a manual dispatcher: its --v0 mode (the default) hands off to v0-rewrite and keeps only the shared scope rules and the rules that apply to every mode. The skills don't compete in routing, because doc-tidy has disable-model-invocation. The overlap is in the rules, which already disagree: doc-tidy says "keep both and report the conflict" and v0-rewrite has no matching rule. The two suites share no prompt.
- ssot-consolidate owns any single fact (value, spec, definition) whose copies span code, config, CI, scripts and docs, or only code and config: it finds every copy, proposes one home and edits after approval. docs-audit owns docs-vs-code drift and duplication that sits only in docs (assigning one owner doc through doc-roles.md), and points mixed-surface single-fact consolidation to ssot-consolidate.
- dotnet-upgrade-guide owns migrating a test framework or runner: xUnit v2 to xunit.v3, MSTest v1/v2/v3 to v3/v4, VSTest to Microsoft.Testing.Platform, and moving between frameworks. That covers the package, project and CI filter changes the move needs, because its test-frameworks references hold that procedure. dotnet-testing owns writing, running, filtering and diagnosing tests on the platform and framework the repo already uses, including the question "VSTest or MTP?" for the current setup. Both bodies already state this split; only the descriptions need to catch up.
- dotnet-performance owns code-level speed work: the measure-first rule, the hot-path gate and scan, BenchmarkDotNet setup and result reading, and SIMD. dotnet-diagnostics owns collecting runtime evidence (counters, traces, dumps, dotnet-monitor, PerfView, perfcollect, container and mobile crash artifacts) from running or crashed processes, and hands slow-code and benchmark requests to dotnet-performance. Both skills' own "Not for" lines already state this split; only dotnet-diagnostics breaks it.
- feature-flags owns work on one flag in code: adding it, evaluating it, testing both paths and removing it (section 4). flag-hygiene owns the read-only, whole-codebase audit: inventory, classification of stale, orphaned and duplicate flags, the registry and the ranked removal list. It hands each removal back to feature-flags, one flag per change.
- mcp-server owns every request to design, build, extend or test an MCP server, including one written in C# with the ModelContextProtocol SDK. Its language-neutral procedure (tool surface, schemas, transport, stdout hygiene, errors, Inspector tests) is the part that does the work. dotnet-ai-apps owns AI and ML inside .NET apps (IChatClient, Agent Framework, RAG, ML.NET, ONNX) and keeps sending C# MCP-server requests to mcp-server.
- doubt-review owns the procedure for refuting an in-flight claim or decision with a fresh-context adversarial reviewer, and it is the skill the model invokes on its own. fresh-eyes stays a manual-only command (disable-model-invocation). Its --disprove mode is the typed entry point to that same procedure and runs doubt-review's cycle rather than keeping its own copy. The routing split already exists because fresh-eyes cannot auto-load. The overlap that matters is the duplicated procedure text, which can drift apart.
- pre-commit owns hook config, install, rev bumps, hook repair, and the hook command a CI job should run (`prek run --all-files`, refs, caching). forgejo-actions owns writing, editing and debugging the workflow YAML on a Forgejo or Codeberg remote, including the job that runs prek and any CI lint step that has nothing to do with hooks. This is the split both skills already describe. The only gap is that pre-commit points to `gh-actions` for CI workflows but never names `forgejo-actions`.
- forgejo-issues owns all Forgejo or Codeberg issue work: reading, searching, creating, editing, labeling, closing and dependencies on issues, plus the issue-side milestone and label lookups its body already covers. forgejo-cli owns the fj tool itself: install, per-host auth, host and remote selection with the -H/-R/-r placement table, the command map and its gaps, the gh-like-client-for-Forgejo request, and any leftover fj task that no narrower forgejo skill covers (wiki, repos, orgs, tags). forgejo-cli points to forgejo-issues for issues, and forgejo-issues keeps pointing back to forgejo-cli when fj is missing or logged out and for the placement table.
- Keep the existing split, which is by forge. gh-pr owns PRs on github.com and on GitHub hosts that gh knows, using gh. forgejo-pr owns PRs on Codeberg and self-hosted Forgejo/Gitea, using fj, plus fork and AGit PRs on those forges. Both descriptions already point at each other with "Not for" clauses, and each body has a forge gate that sends the request to the other skill, so neither needs a boundary change.
- lens-review owns any request to judge one artifact through several lenses, one per failure mode, and return where they agree or disagree plus the one question that settles a split. fresh-eyes keeps only the work that needs a fresh-context subagent (--disprove, --cold, --tunnel). Its --lens mode runs inline by default, which goes against fresh-eyes' own premise, and it repeats lens-review's procedure, which lens-review has in fuller form. So --lens becomes a pointer to lens-review.
- The forge that hosts the landing page decides the owner, as both skills already say. forgejo-readme owns README work for Forgejo, Codeberg and Gitea-style repos. gh-readme owns README work for github.com and hosts that `gh auth` knows. Neither skill owns requests where the forge is unknown. Both findings are really about the third skill, `readme`, so routing between `readme` and these two is a separate decision and is not settled here. The two suites share no prompt.
- game-assets owns game art requests: art style and palette, sprites, animation, tilesets, UI and icon art, asset manifests, image-generation briefs, import settings and asset licenses. game-craft is the engine-neutral hub for the other game topics and handles art only through its references/assets.md fallback when game-assets is not installed.
- game-architecture owns game code structure: game loop and fixed timestep, state machines, composition, event buses, pooling, data-driven content, inventory and ability systems, scene flow and save systems. It is the dedicated skill, it has the workflow, and it has references/patterns.md and references/save-systems.md. game-craft stays the engine-neutral umbrella router, and for architecture and saves it only points to game-architecture.
- game-performance owns every frame-rate request: low FPS, stutter, hitches, frame drops, frame budgets, profiling and performance regression benchmarks. Its body has the full measure-classify-fix-remeasure procedure and a deeper reference. game-craft keeps the other engine-neutral craft topics and sends frame-rate requests to game-performance.
- tunnel-check owns the tunnel-vision check: asking whether the session locked onto its first approach, using 2 to 5 stripped fan-out reads with divergence reported first. Its SKILL.md is the canonical copy of that procedure. fresh-eyes keeps --disprove, --cold and --lens. Its --tunnel flag stays only as a pointer that says to follow tunnel-check, so the steps live in one file.
- game-design owns game design requests: pitches, GDDs, pillars, core loop, mechanic specs, progression, balance curves, difficulty, economy, loot and drop rates, and scope cuts. Its body holds the full procedure for these (artifact table, 7-step workflow, review questions, gotchas). game-craft keeps the other engine-neutral craft topics and points to game-design for design work. Its references/design.md is only the fallback when game-design is not installed.
- game-ai owns all enemy/NPC decision-making: FSMs for AI, behavior trees, blackboards, utility scoring, perception, pathfinding, steering and flocking, AI difficulty knobs, and "the enemy gets stuck". Its body and its references (behavior-trees.md, utility-ai.md, pathfinding.md) hold the procedure, and game-craft's references/ai.md is only a condensed copy of it. game-craft keeps engine-neutral craft requests that span several topics and its other topic rows, and sends single-topic enemy-AI requests to game-ai. Of the shared prompt (guard patrol/chase/search), game-ai/trigger-game-ai-1 stays the positive trigger.
- game-audio owns all engine-neutral game audio requests: bus and mixer layout, dB sliders, loudness targets, ducking, SFX variation and voice limits, adaptive music and beat sync. Its SKILL.md body has the workflow, patterns and gotchas for these, and Haiku already routes these prompts to it. game-craft keeps its other ten topics and sends audio to game-audio. Engine nodes and API stay with godot.
- game-playtest owns every request to plan, run or analyse a playtest: research questions, recruiting, session scripts, observer notes, surveys, playtest telemetry, ranking fixes from playtest findings, and keep-or-kill readouts. Its body has the full 9-step procedure, the session kit and the telemetry reference. game-craft keeps the engine-neutral craft topics and sends playtest requests to game-playtest. A request that only mentions playtest data in passing while asking about feel, performance or saves (e.g. trigger-cross-topic-demo-feedback) stays with game-craft.
- game-feel owns single-topic control-feel requests: floaty or laggy jumps, coyote time, input buffer, deadzones, rebinding, camera follow and shake, juice, hit-stop, and jitter at a steady frame rate. Its body has the workflow and three reference files for this, against game-craft's single 81-line feel.md. game-craft keeps only requests that span several game topics (for example, demo feedback covering feel plus frame rate plus saves) and sends feel-only requests to game-feel.
- game-prototype owns all timeboxed prototyping work: greybox mechanic spikes, vertical slices, keep/kill/retune verdicts on a prototype, and game-jam planning (scope, hour schedule, cut list, submission). Its body has the full procedure, and game-craft's references/prototype.md is a near-verbatim copy of it. game-craft keeps every other engine-neutral craft topic, including level blockout and playtest analysis, and sends prototype and jam requests to game-prototype.
- This is a split by forge. forgejo-pr-comments owns review feedback on Forgejo, Codeberg and Gitea PRs, using fj and forgejo-mcp. pr-comments owns review feedback on GitHub PRs, using gh and fetch.sh. Three things favour this split: forgejo-pr-comments' description already draws this line, the repo pairs skills this way elsewhere (gh-pr/forgejo-pr, ship/forgejo-ship, gh-triage "not for Forgejo"), and forgejo-pr-comments' body already holds the whole Forgejo procedure inline. pr-comments only reaches the Forgejo procedure by sending the reader to references/forgejo.md.
- forgejo-readme owns every README or landing-page request for a repo hosted on Forgejo, Codeberg or Gitea. That matches what each description already claims, and forgejo-readme wins routing on that prompt 6/6. readme keeps README work where the forge is not Forgejo: GitHub (the overlap with gh-readme is a separate pair and is not settled here), no remote or an unknown host, or a README shown on several forges. When readme detects a Forgejo signal, it hands off to forgejo-readme.
- game-feel owns the engine-neutral design and tuning side of feel: why a jump feels floaty, how long coyote time and the input buffer should be, camera follow and shake, juice, and jitter described as a symptom. godot-physics owns the Godot 4 API side: CharacterBody and move_and_slide code, the coyote and buffer code in controllers.md, physics interpolation settings, get_global_transform_interpolated and reset_physics_interpolation. A jitter request that names Godot nodes or Godot settings goes to godot-physics. The same complaint with no engine named goes to game-feel.
- level-design owns every level request: layout, blockout of a level, critical path and gating, pacing and encounters, and seeded procedural level generation (dungeons, caves, BSP, WFC, sub-seeds). It has the full workflow plus the pacing-encounters.md and procgen.md references. game-craft stays the engine-neutral umbrella for its other topics and sends level requests to `level-design` rather than keeping its own condensed copy.
- godot-addons owns choosing, installing, enabling, upgrading and writing game code or .dialogue files against the four third-party addons it names (Beehave, LimboAI, Phantom Camera, Dialogue Manager). godot-editor-tools owns writing or fixing the project's own editor plugin under addons/<name>/ (EditorPlugin, plugin.cfg, @tool scripts, inspector plugins, docks, gizmos, undo/redo), and the mere presence of an addons/*/plugin.cfg is not a trigger for it.
- git-flow owns work in repos on the git-flow model (main plus develop, feature/release/hotfix/support branches, git-flow-next, AVH or plain git). trunk-based owns work in trunk-based repos (short-lived branches, feature flags, branch by abstraction, late-cut release branches with cherry-picks, release from trunk). Neither owns the generic question of which branching model to choose: that goes to branching-models, whose description already claims it. Each skill keeps its short "When to use this model" section only to redirect when the repo turns out to use the other model.
- game-ui owns all game UI and UX requests: HUDs, menus, pause and settings screens, the screen stack, scaling and safe areas, gamepad focus, localization-ready layout, world-space markers, and game accessibility (text size, subtitles, remapping, colour, motion and flash). Its body has the step-by-step procedure, patterns, gotchas and two references for this. game-craft stays the engine-neutral router for the other game topics and sends UI requests to game-ui. Web or app UI belongs to neither skill; both point to the design skills.
- trunk-based owns release policy in a trunk-based repo: where a fix lands, fixing on trunk first and then cherry-picking to a late-cut release/X.Y, never merging the release branch back, and when to cut or delete release branches. git-history owns the git mechanics in any repo: rewriting, rebasing, cherry-pick -x and backport commands (on a branch made for the backport), bisect, and reflog recovery. The two suites share no prompt, so every eval case stays where it is.
- `readme` owns every README request: write, audit, restructure and beautify a repo's README or front page on GitHub, Forgejo, Codeberg or Gitea. Its body does everything gh-readme does and also detects the forge first, which matters because most prompts never name a forge, so the GitHub-only split can't be told apart at routing time. gh-readme is retired and keeps no trigger.
- godot owns standalone `@tool` scripts on game nodes: editor previews, setters, `_draw`, `Engine.is_editor_hint()` guards, configuration warnings and one-off `EditorScript`s. godot-editor-tools owns everything under `addons/<name>/` with `plugin.cfg`: EditorPlugin, docks, tool menu items, inspector plugins, gizmos, custom types, servers inside the editor, and any tool code that edits the open scene through undo/redo and `owner`. The two eval suites share no prompt. The implicit 'Scatter button loses nodes on save / no undo' case stays a positive trigger for godot-editor-tools, because the undo/redo and owner procedure lives there.
- godot-export owns producing the dedicated-server build: the "Export as dedicated server" preset, stripping textures and meshes, and the headless CLI export command. godot-multiplayer owns everything about running that server: starting without a window, choosing server or client code at boot (dedicated_server tag versus --headless), reading the port and other settings from the command line, match flow, and deploying with Docker or systemd. The two suites share no prompt. trigger-godot-multiplayer-2 (Docker, boot branching, command-line port) stays a positive trigger in godot-multiplayer, and godot-export needs no eval changes.
- goff-relay-proxy owns every GO Feature Flag relay proxy request: configuring goff-proxy.yaml, retrievers, exporters and notifiers, authorizedKeys and admin keys, flagSets, refresh, Docker, Helm, Kubernetes, and debugging the proxy. Its body has the configure, run, deploy and debug procedure. goff keeps only flag files and SDK wiring, and points proxy work to goff-relay-proxy.
- goff-sdk owns all app-code work for GO Feature Flag: OpenFeature providers (server, client, mobile), the Go `ffclient` module, OFREP, evaluation context and targetingKey, tracking from SDKs, and SDK tests. Its body has the full procedure for this (integration table, evaluation modes, tracking and export, test steps). goff keeps flag files and the relay proxy, and sends SDK requests to goff-sdk.
- goff-flags owns every request about GO Feature Flag flag files: writing, reviewing or debugging `*.goff.yaml`/JSON/TOML flags, targeting queries, rollouts, bucketingKey and percentage behaviour, and `go-feature-flag-cli` lint/evaluate/manifest. goff keeps the relay proxy and OpenFeature SDK/provider wiring, and sends flag-file work to goff-flags. Of the two descriptions, only goff-flags draws this boundary. Its body holds the full procedure (rules, authoring flow, CLI verification, review checklist), and in routing runs it beat goff every time it competed.
- implement-plan owns every "implement this plan" / "continue implementing" / "carry out this plan file" request; it is the default way to execute a plan file. subagent-workflows owns that job only when the user explicitly asks for a SubagentWorkflow run, or names plan-slice-implement, for example after a feature-plan workflow run. In that case it covers running plan-slice-implement (its args, committed plan, clean tree, gateCmd) and does not authorize starting the run unasked.
- jetpack-compose owns writing, reviewing and debugging Compose code: state, effects, component APIs, lists, theming, animation, focus and previews. uiux-lookup owns only offline lookups of one cited UX rule or one dated guideline row, including rows from its `jetpack-compose` stack. An example is "minimum touch target on Android".
- postmortem owns the incident document: the timeline, impact, detection gap, 5 Whys, and owned, dated actions, whether writing it or reviewing it. mistake-proof owns the code fix that comes after: it separates defect, mistake and hazard, designs a device that removes the hazard, places it on the control/warning/detection ladder, and sweeps the repo for the same shape. That keeps the split each body already describes. The suites share no prompt, so no eval cases move.
- spring-boot owns everything about Spring and JPA that is not specific to Kotlin: transactions, fetching, N+1, pagination, bulk updates, locking, uniqueness and open-in-view. kotlin owns only what changes when that code is written in Kotlin: the plugin.spring and plugin.jpa setup, regular classes instead of data class entities, the nullable id, equality and hashCode, @field: annotation targets, suspend controllers, and data class DTOs. For the general JPA questions, kotlin points to spring-boot.
- production-readiness owns the repo-wide ship-or-block review: whether something is ready to ship, covering security, secrets, CORS, rate limits, dependency scanning, env validation, observability and migrations, and ending in a Blocked, Risky or Caveats verdict. rollout-plan owns how a known change goes out: picking a strategy, preflight go/no-go, verification signals, numeric rollback criteria, judging whether a running deploy is healthy, and deciding to roll back. Both descriptions already state this split, so it stays as it is.
- privacy-review owns questions about where personal data goes and whether each copy is minimized, kept for a set time, erasable and exportable: PII inventory, flows to logs, telemetry and third parties, and erasure and export. threat-model owns attacker-centred work, even on systems that hold PII: STRIDE, trust boundaries, data-flow diagrams, attack trees, exploitability tiers and baseline reruns. Neither suite has a copy of the other's prompt. Each suite already has a mirrored negative (privacy-review/route-negative-threat-model-customer-table routes to threat-model; threat-model/route-negative-personal-data-inventory routes to privacy-review), and both stay as they are.

Measure first, then cut the largest contributor. Read `references/size.md` before ruling on any size proposal: it covers APK Analyzer and `apkanalyzer`, download size vs install size, resource shrinking, native libraries and ABIs, and the order to attack them. Rulings that are easy to get wrong:

- Keep native libraries uncompressed (`useLegacyPackaging = false`): the uploaded artifact is larger, but the Play download and the install are smaller. Do not compress them to save size.
- For an AAB, Play already splits by ABI, density and language, so `abiFilters` and locale filters barely change a user's download; they shrink the universal or sideloaded APK.
- Never combine `splits { abi }` with a bundle upload.

Feature triage for every idea, first match wins: the loop does not work without it, so build it now; the loop works without it and a player would not notice it missing, so cut it; a player would notice it and it takes under 30 minutes, so it is a stretch goal, built only before the feature freeze; otherwise cut it for the jam and note it for a post-jam update. Under deadline pressure the default answer is cut.

# GO Feature Flag

GO Feature Flag (GOFF) flags live in a YAML, JSON or TOML file. A relay proxy loads it through retrievers and serves it over HTTP and OFREP. Apps evaluate through an OpenFeature SDK plus a GOFF provider; Go-only apps may embed the Go module instead. Facts here come from the GOFF docs (v1.58.1) and repo files; nothing was run against a live proxy, and items marked verify are unconfirmed.

Vendor-neutral flag practice (design, testing both states, removal) is the `feature-flags` skill; repo-wide stale-flag audits are the `flag-hygiene` skill.

## Route the task

- Flag files (fields, queries, rollouts, lint/evaluate): use the `goff-flags` skill.
- Relay proxy setup, deployment and debugging: use the `goff-relay-proxy` skill.
- App-code and provider work (OpenFeature providers, the Go `ffclient` module, OFREP): use the `goff-sdk` skill.

## Facts that apply everywhere

- `targetingKey` is mandatory in every evaluation context (missing gives `TARGETING_KEY_MISSING`) and must be a stable unique id (user, session), not a random value per request.
- Only attributes in the context reach a query; a missing attribute means the rule does not match.
- The context key `gofeatureflag` is reserved (`currentDateTime`, `flagList`, `exporterMetadata`); never use it for your own data.
- The proxy's `evaluationContextEnrichment` is merged into every context and overrides same-named fields.
- Pass `apiKey` when the proxy has `authorizedKeys` or flagSets; a flagSet request without a key fails.
END

4. `flowOn` moves the upstream, not the collector. `catch` handles upstream errors only, so put it before `collect`/`launchIn` and rethrow cancellation. An exception thrown inside `collect { }` is not seen by `catch`; move the work into `onEach { }` and write `.onEach { }.catch { }.collect()`.

Replace with:
Before Kotlin 2.4 an annotation on a constructor `val` goes only to the parameter; from 2.4 (or with `-Xannotation-default-target=param-property` on 2.2+) it goes to the parameter and the property, or the field when the property target does not apply. Check the Kotlin version first, and write the target explicitly when the framework reads a field or getter: `@field:Column`, `@get:JsonProperty`, `@param:Inject`, `@set:`. A Bean Validation annotation that is silently ignored is usually on the wrong target (`@field:NotBlank`, `@get:NotBlank`).

**New description:** Audits an eval, metric, experiment or benchmark for leakage and reports which independence checks fail, each with a fix. Use when asked "is this A/B actually measuring anything?", "is the grader the same model a problem?", "is this holdout clean?", before reporting a score whose outputs and judging (or test set and tuning) came from the same model or person, or when a result is better than anyone expected. # Metals language server

Contents: prerequisites, first start, troubleshooting, security.

This applies only when the host provides a Metals or LSP tool, or the user asks to set Metals up. Without one, find symbols with Grep and compile with the build tool.

## Prerequisites

Checked against the Metals docs on 2026-10-20 (latest stable 1.6.9, released 2026-09-14):

1. A JDK for the Metals server. The minimum is 11; the VS Code docs list 11, 17 and 21 with 17 as the default. Metals uses `JAVA_HOME` if set. The project's own JDK (what sbt and Mill use) is separate and also comes from `JAVA_HOME` unless the `javaHome` setting overrides it.
2. Coursier (`cs`), https://get-coursier.io.
3. Install Metals and put it on the PATH:

   ```sh
   cs install metals            # installs a `metals` launcher into the coursier bin dir
   cs bootstrap org.scalameta:metals_2.13:1.6.9 -o metals -f   # alternative: pin a version
   ```

   The coursier bin dir (`cs install` prints it; usually `~/.local/share/coursier/bin`) must be on the PATH of the process that starts the language server. Check with `command -v metals`.
4. A buildable project: an sbt, Mill, Maven, Gradle or Bazel build, or Scala CLI files. Metals imports through Bloop (Mill: automatic via Bloop) or the build's own BSP support.

## First start

Metals imports the build and indexes it before diagnostics and symbol search work, so the first start in a project can take minutes. Until the import and first compile finish, Metals reports parser-only `scalameta` diagnostics, which can be wrong for Scala 3 syntax.

- The import needs `sbt` to run from the environment the server inherits. A `mise` shim without an active version fails there; check `sbt --version` in the project directory first. A second sbt on the same machine can hold `~/.ivy2/.sbt.ivy.lock` and stall the import (`waiting for lock`).
- To import by hand (for example for a build that needs special flags), run `sbt -Dbloop.export-jar-classifiers=sources bloopInstall` once (needs the sbt-bloop plugin; checked against scalameta.org/metals/docs/build-tools/sbt on 2026-10-20) and Metals connects to Bloop on its next start.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| No server for `.scala` files | `command -v metals` in the shell that started the client; fix the PATH and restart |
| `metals: command not found` | the coursier bin dir is missing from PATH |
| Starts, then no diagnostics | the build import has not finished or failed; run the build tool in the project and look at `.metals/metals.log` |
| Wrong Scala or Java | `JAVA_HOME`, `scalaVersion`, the `javaHome` setting |
| Crash loop | delete `.metals/` and `.bloop/` in the project and retry |

Metals writes `.metals/`, `.bloop/` and `project/metals.sbt` into the project. Make sure they are in `.gitignore` before committing.

## Security

A build import runs sbt, Bloop or the project's other build tool, which executes the project's build definition (`build.sbt`, plugins, `build.mill`) and any `.bsp/*.json` build server command. Only import projects you trust, as with any IDE import.

- `toString`, logging, JSON serialization and IDE debugger inspection can trigger lazy loads; keep lazy associations out of `toString`.
- Use a `@Version` field for optimistic locking.
- Enforce uniqueness with a database unique constraint, because an application-side check races. Add a lookup only to give a clean error instead of a raw `DataIntegrityViolationException`.

- A collection fetch join (`join fetch` or `@EntityGraph` on a collection) combined with pagination loads every row into memory and pages there; fetching several bags (`List` collections) at once multiplies rows. Page the parent ids first, then fetch the collections for those ids.
